column1: Tell me about yourself / Walk me through your background
column2: I'm a full-stack software engineer with about 5 years of experience. I started back in college, in 2021, already freelancing while studying Information Systems — that was my first real taste of production work, juggling React, Vue, Next, and Laravel while still in school. Almost 3 years ago I joined A4PM, a public healthtech company, and worked my way up from UI tasks to owning entire features across a 4-system ecosystem — today I work on an EHR with over 10 years of history, 1,300+ tables, 6 versions running in production at the same time. My senior thesis turned into a real product too, Mirante Social. Right now I'm looking for a new step because I feel I've explored what A4PM had to offer, and I want an environment that pushes me toward a different level of complexity than what I already have down.

column1: What's your hands-on experience with [technology X]?
column2: I use it both at A4PM and in personal/freelance projects. But what I really bring to the table isn't years with a specific library — it's understanding the problem underneath it: state architecture, performance trade-offs, that kind of thing transfers from one stack to another. I started much stronger in PHP/Laravel and today I'm just as fluent in Node/TypeScript/React — and that wasn't an accident, I deliberately picked up new stacks whenever a project called for it instead of staying comfortable in just one.

column1: How was your education, and why did you choose this field?
column2: I studied Information Systems at CEFET/RJ, between 2021 and 2025, and the choice came from already liking logical problem-solving before college. The difference is I didn't stay in theory — I started freelancing in the first year of the program, so my education and hands-on experience ran in parallel the whole time, not one after the other. My thesis turned into a real production project, Mirante Social, which reinforced that bridge between studying and applying it.

column1: Why are you leaving your current job?
column2: It's not that I'm unhappy there — quite the opposite, I've learned a lot in almost 3 years at A4PM. But I feel like I've absorbed most of what the company had to offer at this point, I know that ecosystem well, and now I'm looking for a new challenge, a different product context to keep growing technically and test my level somewhere else.

column1: Why do you want to work here / in this role specifically?
column2: Two reasons. First, the technical challenge itself — [adapt: the stack, the domain, the product's scale] appeals to me because it connects directly with the kind of problem I've actually solved before, so I'd come in contributing, not just learning from scratch. Second, the timing — I'm looking for a new environment after almost 3 years consolidating a lot at a single company, and this role looks like the right kind of jump: challenging enough to keep me growing, but within things I already do well.

column1: What are you looking for in your next position?
column2: I'm looking for more ownership over architecture decisions — not just implementing what's already been decided, but being at the table from the initial design. And I want a team that already treats AI as a natural part of the workflow, not as a suspicious novelty — that changed my delivery speed a lot without sacrificing quality, and I'd rather be somewhere that already sees it as an advantage, not a shortcut.

column1: Have you thought about starting your own business or going fully freelance?
column2: I've been freelancing alongside my full-time job since 2021 — shipped a B2B SaaS, a language-learning platform, payment integrations, LLM integrations. I like using that as a lab for stacks and approaches I don't use day to day, without the risk of touching critical production. But I'd rather keep that as a complement, not a replacement for a stable position — what really draws me is the long-term impact of a mature product in production, and freelancing alone doesn't give me that.

column1: What's your biggest weakness / what are you still working on?
column2: One weakness of mine is dealing with slower, more bureaucratic process. For example, when I have a bug to fix or a feature to ship, I study the scenario, align quickly with whoever needs it, and jump straight into building. As soon as I'm done, I want to open the PR, and I get a bit anxious waiting for QA. But sometimes testing, retesting, and documentation takes several days, with adjustments nobody saw coming at the start. That makes me a little impatient — but it's something I've been working on, understanding that not everything is under my control and that time is also part of delivering with quality.

column1: What's your biggest strength?
column2: My biggest strength is being able to jump into a large, complex legacy system — in my case, an EHR with over 10 years of code and 1,300+ tables — and quickly figure out where it's safe to make changes. That comes from doing production on-call there, where I had to triage critical tickets and ship deploys across 135+ health units without breaking anything. That built a discipline of reading unfamiliar code fast, prioritizing by real risk, and communicating that clearly before acting.

column1: How do you handle feedback or criticism on your code or decisions?
column2: I separate the technical point from my ego pretty fast — the goal is for the system to get better, not for me to "win" the discussion. If the point raised is well-grounded, I incorporate it without drama. When I disagree, I don't respond with opinion against opinion — I bring the concrete scenario that led me to that decision, including what I already ruled out and why, because the criticism usually comes from someone who didn't see that part of the analysis. That tends to resolve fast, because it turns into "let's compare both paths with this extra context" instead of a clash of preferences.

column1: Describe a conflict with a coworker over a technical approach
column2: I once disagreed on how to structure an integration — I wanted to isolate the external logic behind its own layer, my coworker preferred wiring it directly into the existing flow to save time. Instead of pushing my opinion, I proposed quickly prototyping both approaches and comparing what would happen if the external API changed or failed. That grounded the decision in actual risk instead of preference — we ended up going with the isolated layer, which really did save us rework later when that integration had to change.

column1: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager or tech lead
column2: I once disagreed on a priority call — leadership wanted to ship a new feature before addressing technical debt I saw growing in a critical module. Instead of just accepting it or digging in stubbornly, I pulled up the ticket history tied to that area to show it wasn't just me being difficult, it was a pattern. And I didn't just show up complaining — I proposed a middle ground: ship the feature in parallel with a minimal fix that already relieved most of the risk, leaving the full fix for later. It was accepted easily because it turned into a priority conversation backed by data, not stubbornness versus stubbornness.

column1: How do you work with people of very different seniority or background than yours?
column2: I change the level of the conversation, not the substance. With someone more junior, I spend more time explaining the "why" behind a decision than the "what" — otherwise they just copy the pattern without understanding when it stops applying. With product or design, I barely talk about implementation at all, I talk trade-offs and impact in terms that matter to them. I've done a lot of that mentoring newer engineers at A4PM on the architecture patterns we use — what works well is never assuming everyone already sees the problem the way I do.

column1: Tell me about a hard technical problem you solved
column2: I had a case with a real-time dashboard over WebSocket that was originally designed for light load — it started out serving around 2 tenants — and once it scaled to around 30, it started visibly lagging, a few seconds per event. The cause was the real-time connection state sitting in a single Context with no selector: every event re-rendered the entire tree, even cards that had nothing to do with that specific piece of data. I had three options: split into multiple Contexts by domain, switch to a store with atomic selectors, or reduce event frequency at the source. I ruled out multiple Contexts because it just pushes the problem down the road — it would still scale badly as the number of cards grew. I went with a store using atomic selectors on the front end, so each card only subscribes to the slice it uses, combined with batching nearby events into a short window on the backend before emitting them. That fixed both sides of the problem — render volume and event volume — and the dashboard handled the real growth that came afterward just fine. It made it clear to me that real-time bottlenecks are almost always a data-contract problem, not just a rendering one.

column1: Tell me about a complex integration you've built with an external system
column2: I integrated our shared care flow with RNDS, Brazil's national health data network — a platform with 2.8 billion records, over Apache Thrift using the FHIR/HL7 standard. The challenge was ensuring regulatory compliance without breaking production care flows. I studied the protocol closely, mapped failure points like timeouts and malformed data coming from outside my control, and built defensive error handling so an external failure would never take down the internal flow. It's been running in production without incidents since.

column1: Have you had to debug something hard to reproduce? How did you approach it?
column2: A lot, mostly in large legacy systems — in my case, an EHR with over 10 years of code. My approach is to isolate variable by variable: first confirm it reproduces in a controlled environment, then check if it's specific to one unit/tenant or something general, then keep narrowing scope until I find the root cause, instead of changing code by guesswork. I write down the path I took, even informally — in a system with lots of people touching it, the same kind of bug tends to resurface elsewhere months later, and having that trail saves a lot of investigation time.

column1: How do you decide between a quick fix and doing it right (refactoring)?
column2: I weigh blast radius and how often that piece of code gets touched before deciding. I've seen up close what it costs to get this wrong: a coworker, under deadline pressure, fixed a duplicate-record issue in one of our clinical modules by filtering the duplicate out on the screen, without addressing the root cause at the point where the data was written — and without documenting any of it. Months later, another flow started consuming that same data directly from the database, bypassing that screen, and the duplication came back, this time affecting an official report — a much more serious context to fix after the fact. Since then my bar is stricter: if it's isolated, low risk, and I document the debt with a review date, it's fine to move fast. If the data or flow could be consumed from more than one place — which is almost always true in a system with 1,300+ tables — I insist on fixing it at the source, because a silent quick fix there doesn't stay isolated, it spreads.

column1: Tell me about a time you mentored or helped someone more junior
column2: I onboard new engineers at A4PM on the architecture patterns we use, like HMVC and Clean Architecture, in a system with over 10 years of history and a lot of implicit convention that's not documented anywhere. Instead of just handing over a list of rules, I explain the historical "why" behind each convention — a lot of it exists because of an old decision that made sense in its own context — because understanding the origin helps someone generalize the pattern to new situations instead of just memorizing rules.

column1: Tell me about an initiative you took that had real impact, without anyone asking for it
column2: I adopted AI-assisted development in a structured way in my workflow — not just asking for ready-made code, but speeding up problem exploration, test writing, and pattern review. Nobody asked for this formally, I started applying it on my own, and the result was cutting feature delivery time from 1-2 weeks down to 2-3 days, without an increase in incidents. Today I help spread that practice to other engineers on the team, so it turned into a collective gain, not just a personal one.

column1: Have you ever disagreed with a product decision and had to implement it anyway?
column2: Yes. In those moments I state my concern once, directly and without drama, usually pointing out the specific risk I see — performance, future maintainability, that kind of thing. But once the decision is made, I don't spend the implementation "proving I was right" — I execute it with the same care as if it were my own idea. Implementing something half-heartedly only makes the product worse without changing the decision, so I don't see the point in that.

column1: How do you handle tight deadlines versus pressure for quality?
column2: I try never to let it become "me against the deadline" — I show the business side the real cost of cutting corners, not as technical stubbornness, but as "this is going to come back as a problem in a few weeks, I'd rather we decide that with eyes open." I'd rather negotiate scope or deadline openly with the client/PO than ship something patched together just to hit a date. When cutting something really can't be avoided, I write it down somewhere visible with a review date — the problem is never cutting a corner once, it's that becoming a silent habit.

column1: Tell me about a real mistake you made in production and what you learned
column2: I had a case on the SUS Transparency Portal, a project I lead — a real-time dashboard, updated via a GraphQL subscription, started re-rendering the entire tree on every incoming event, because the real-time connection state was sitting close to the root component. It didn't take the system down, but it visibly degraded performance for the user. I fixed it by isolating that state in a dedicated child component, with memoization on the rest of the tree. The lesson was that high-frequency state needs to live as close as possible to whoever actually uses it — I think about that from the initial design now, not just when the problem shows up.

column1: How do you react when you find out you shipped a mistake to production?
column2: First I communicate it as soon as possible, without trying to downplay or hide it — the sooner the team knows, the smaller the blast radius. Then I focus on containing the problem (rollback, hotfix, or temporary mitigation) before calmly investigating the root cause. Only after it's resolved do I review what was missing in the process — testing, review, staging environment — to reduce the chance of it repeating, instead of treating it as isolated individual blame.

column1: Tell me about a time you had to make a technical decision with incomplete information
column2: That's pretty much routine in legacy systems, where a lot of the business rules only live in the heads of whoever worked on it before. In those cases I don't try to get it perfectly right the first time — I pick the option that's easiest to undo if my assumption turns out wrong, instead of a "perfect" but rigid solution that locks me in if I misunderstood something. And I write down, even informally, what assumption I made — that's saved me from serious rework more than once, because someone who knew that flow better caught the gap before it became a production problem.

column1: How do you stay technically up to date?
column2: These days I use AI quite a bit in a structured way in my workflow — Claude Code, MCP — not just to generate code, but to speed up problem exploration and pattern review. And the personal/freelance projects I keep running alongside my main job work as a testing ground for stacks and approaches I don't use day to day — that's where I fail fast and learn without the risk of touching critical production.

column1: Do you prefer remote, hybrid, or in-person work? Why?
column2: I prefer remote — I've worked that way for almost 3 years and built my own discipline around async communication and time management, without needing in-person supervision to stay productive. What I actually value isn't the location itself, it's having clear communication channels with the team and sync meetings that are actually used well, only when they add something — not out of habit.

column1: What motivates you day to day as a software engineer?
column2: I especially like taking a complex system, often legacy, and really understanding how it works under the hood before touching it — there's real satisfaction in solving a problem that requires understanding historical context, not just applying a generic pattern. I also like the mentoring side of it, watching someone more junior unlock a concept I helped explain.

column1: How much do you currently make?
column2: I'd rather not anchor to my current salary because I feel like I'm in a position that's pretty misaligned with what I deliver and what the market pays today — that's why my expectation for this next step is based on what I consider fair for the level of work I do, not what I currently make.

column1: What would your timeline be to start?
column2: I'd need about two weeks of transition — handing off my current responsibilities to the team and documenting processes that only I currently own, so I don't leave anyone hanging on my way out. It's not about bureaucracy, it's about leaving in a way that doesn't create debt for the team that stays.

column1: Do you have any restrictions on hours, time zone, or availability?
column2: No relevant restrictions — I already work remote and have dealt with different time zones before when a project called for it. I adapt well to an overlap window, as long as it's clearly agreed on upfront.

column1: Where do you see yourself in 5 years?
column2: I see myself in a role with a lot more technical ownership than I have today — involved from the architecture design stage, not just implementation. Not necessarily as a people manager, that's not what draws me most
column3: I want to keep growing as a technical reference, something like a staff or principal engineer, someone the team calls in when the decision is big and has a lot of trade-offs involved. The path I've been on — from UI work to owning an entire system at A4PM — is already heading that way, I just want to keep accelerating it.

column1: Why should we hire you? What sets you apart from other candidates?
column2: I think the differentiator is the combination of having already solved real scale problems — a system with over 10 years of history, 1,300+ tables, integration with a federal platform holding 2.8 billion records — with the fact that I turned that into being a reference inside the team, not just delivering solo. I don't just show up knowing code, I show up knowing how to communicate risk, mentor people who are just starting out, and make decisions even with incomplete information, which is the reality of any large system in production.

column1: How do you work under minimal supervision, without someone checking every step?
column2: I've been working that way for almost 3 years, remote, at A4PM — my direct manager doesn't track lines of code, he tracks delivery and communication. What works for me is being clear early about what I'm doing and flagging blockers fast, instead of disappearing until I solve it myself or get fully stuck. I'd rather report "I'm at this point, I hit this obstacle" early than only show up at the end with an unsolved problem.

column1: How do you handle multiple priorities at the same time?
column2: Production on-call really taught me this — a poorly triaged ticket turns into a fire, and a real one that's ignored does too, so you can't treat everything as equally urgent. I look at actual impact and risk for each thing, not who asked the loudest. When two genuinely urgent things compete for the same time, I'd rather negotiate that directly with whoever asked than try to do both in parallel and deliver both poorly.

column1: Tell me about a time you had to convince a non-technical person (product, client) of a technical decision
column2: I once had to explain to the business side why we couldn't just plug an external integration directly into the main flow without a protective layer in between. Instead of saying "circuit breaker" or "abstraction layer," I used the scenario that actually mattered to them: "if this government API goes down for 10 minutes, without this layer the entire care flow stops
column3: with it, only that small piece goes down." That unlocked the conversation immediately, because it stopped being an abstract technical decision and became a simple risk question: would you rather everything stops, or just one small part?

column1: Have you ever had to say "no" or deliver bad news about a deadline or scope?
column2: Yes, and the rule I follow is to never show up with just the "no." I once had to say a requested deadline wasn't viable without cutting quality or raising production risk — but I came with what I could deliver in that timeframe and what would move to a second phase. That changes the conversation from "he doesn't want to do it" to "he already thought this through and brought a path forward," and it preserves trust even while delivering bad news.

column1: How do you work with ambiguous or frequently changing requirements?
column2: I don't wait for requirements to be 100% locked down before starting — that almost never really happens. I start with the part that's already clear, building it in a way that's cheap to change later, and I avoid any hard-to-reverse decision upfront. If there's an ambiguity that actually changes the direction of the solution, I ask specifically about that, instead of trying to clarify everything at once — because that usually just stalls the start of the work for no reason.

column1: Tell me about a time you had to learn something completely new, fast
column2: At A4PM, we needed to integrate a module with a message queue the team hadn't used before — I only had theoretical knowledge of it, had never put it in production. Instead of trying to become an expert before starting, I went straight for what changed my way of thinking the most compared to what I already knew — my focus was understanding the key concepts that shifted my reasoning from synchronous request-response to decoupled, asynchronous processing — and I practiced with a small, real case in parallel, instead of just reading the entire documentation before coding. I didn't come out an expert overnight, but I came out able to ship something functional and correct on the timeline the project needed. That's how I approach new technology: focus first on what unlocks the ability to deliver, not on mastering everything before starting.

column1: How do you organize and prioritize your own tasks day to day?
column2: First I look at what someone else is waiting on from me — blocking a teammate down the chain costs a lot more than my own isolated task slipping a bit. Beyond that, I like slicing big tasks into pieces I can validate quickly, instead of disappearing for days without a single checkpoint — that way, if I took the wrong path, I find out early instead of only at the end.

column1: Tell me about a work experience or project that didn't go well
column2: There was a freelance project where I agreed to a shorter deadline than I should have, trying not to lose the client — partway through it became clear the agreed scope didn't fit that timeline without sacrificing quality. I had to go back and renegotiate the deadline mid-project, which is a lot more uncomfortable than adjusting it upfront. I learned I should have aligned scope and deadline more rigorously right at the proposal stage, instead of trying to sort it out "on the fly" — since then, I review scope versus deadline much more carefully before closing any new project, freelance or not.

column1: Do you have any questions for me? (about the team/product)
column2: I do — how is the engineering team structured today, are you in a growth phase or more backfilling right now? And how do architecture decisions get made day to day — is it more centralized with a specific senior person, or does the whole team weigh in on those discussions?

column1: Do you have any questions for me? (about the process/next steps)
column2: I do — what do the next steps look like from here, and what's the rough timeline for hearing back? I like understanding that so I can plan around any other conversations I might have going on at the same time.
